note.explanation: Isotopes have the same number of protons and electrons but different numbers of neutrons. Their electron arrangements are the same, so their chemical behaviour is almost the same; their different masses can give them different physical properties.
examples: ¹²₆C and ¹⁴₆C are isotopes of carbon: each has 6 protons, but they have 6 and 8 neutrons respectively.
Tritium, ³₁H, is radioactive; hydrogen, ¹₁H, and deuterium, ²₁H, are stable.
note.checkAnswer: Isotopes have the same number of electrons, so they show almost the same chemical behaviour. Their different numbers of neutrons give them different masses and physical properties.
note.simple: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. They react almost alike, but their different masses can make some physical properties different.
note.checkQuestion: Why can isotopes of the same element have different masses?
note.title: Isotopes, radioactivity and their uses
steps: Find the element's atomic number: this gives the number of protons.
For a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
Find neutrons by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number.
For a relative atomic mass, multiply each isotope's mass by its percentage abundance, add the results, and divide by 100 when the abundances are percentages.
note.answer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Their chemical properties are almost the same, while their physical properties may differ.

options: They have the same number of protons and electrons but different numbers of neutrons.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes two isotopes of the same element?
rationales: Correct: isotopes of an element have the same atomic number and different neutron numbers.
Incorrect: different proton numbers would mean different elements.
Incorrect: isotopes of a neutral element have the same electron number, and their mass numbers may differ.
Incorrect: different atomic numbers mean different elements, not isotopes.

options: Almost the same chemical behaviour because they have the same number of electrons.
Different chemical behaviour because they have different numbers of neutrons.
Exactly the same physical properties because they are the same element.
Different chemical behaviour because they have different atomic numbers.
mcqs.stem: Why do isotopes of an element show almost the same chemical behaviour?
rationales: Correct: chemical properties depend on electrons, and isotopes have the same number of electrons.
Incorrect: neutron number differs, but it is not what determines chemical properties.
Incorrect: isotopes can have different physical properties because their masses differ.
Incorrect: isotopes have the same atomic number.

rationales: Correct: neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 37 − 17 = 20.
Incorrect: this is not the result of subtracting 17 from 37.
Incorrect: this does not follow from the given mass and atomic numbers.
Incorrect: this does not follow from the given mass and atomic numbers.

options: The nuclei of some isotopes are unstable and emit excess energy as radiation.
Their electrons move into higher shells.
Their atoms absorb visible light.
Their protons turn into electrons in every atom.
mcqs.stem: What causes a radioactive isotope to emit radiation?
rationales: Correct: an unstable nucleus emits excess energy in the form of radiation.
Incorrect: electron-shell changes are not the cause of radioactivity described here.
Incorrect: absorption of visible light is not the stated cause of radioactive emission.
Incorrect: the section does not say that protons turn into electrons in every atom.

options: It changes into another chemical element.
It changes into a different isotope of the same element every time.
It becomes a neutral atom by gaining electrons.
It stops having a nucleus.
mcqs.stem: What happens to a radioactive element when it undergoes radioactive decay?
rationales: Correct: radioactive decay transforms the element into another chemical element.
Incorrect: the text defines radioactive decay as transformation into another element.
Incorrect: the text describes emission and transformation, not electron gain as the defining event.
Incorrect: radioactive decay does not mean the atom loses its nucleus.

options: It can help calculate when an organic sample from a once-living thing died.
It identifies the exact elements in any metal sample.
It measures how strong a concrete mixture is.
It shows whether a sample contains any electrons.
mcqs.stem: What information can radiocarbon dating provide?
rationales: Correct: measuring the amount of carbon-14 in organic material helps calculate its age.
Incorrect: radiocarbon dating is described as an age-finding method, not an elemental analysis method.
Incorrect: radioactive isotopes can test material strength, but that is not radiocarbon dating.
Incorrect: radiocarbon dating does not test for electrons.

A radioactive fluid is used to make the patient's organs radioactive permanently.

A metal detector measures the patient's bones.
mcqs.stem: How can technetium-99m be used in medical imaging, according to the section?
rationales: Correct: the text describes injecting a small amount of radioactive fluid and watching it with a special camera.
Incorrect: the section describes a small diagnostic amount and does not say it makes organs permanently radioactive.
Incorrect: the described technique uses radioactive fluid.
Incorrect: a metal detector is not the imaging method described.

mcqs.stem: What may happen when ionizing radiation hits a sodium atom with enough energy?
rationales: Correct: radiation can force an electron away, leaving a positively charged cation.
Incorrect: the section describes removal of electrons, not addition of protons.
Incorrect: neutron removal is not the ionization process described, and the stated charge is wrong.
Incorrect: losing an electron forms a cation, not a neutral molecule.

written.text: Why does a radioactive isotope emit radiation?
written.finalAnswer: A radioactive isotope has an unstable nucleus. It emits excess energy in the form of radiation.

written.text: Give an example of a radioactive isotope which disintegrates to give a stable atom.
written.finalAnswer: ²¹⁰₈₃Bi disintegrates to give ²⁰⁶₈₁Tl and energy.

rubric.why: The example must identify a radioactive isotope shown in the section.
rubric.how: Give bismuth-210, ²¹⁰₈₃Bi.

rubric.why: The question asks for the stable product of its disintegration.
rubric.how: Give thallium-206, ²⁰⁶₈₁Tl.

modelAnswer: ²¹⁰₈₃Bi → ²⁰⁶₈₁Tl + energy.
Therefore, bismuth-210 disintegrates to give thallium-206, a stable atom.

written.text: Why is tritium (³₁H) a radioactive element?
written.finalAnswer: Tritium (³₁H) has an unstable nucleus, so it emits radiation; the other two hydrogen isotopes are stable.

rubric.how: State that the nucleus of tritium is unstable.

written.text: Why the nuclei of the radioactive elements are unstable?
written.finalAnswer: Radioactive nuclei are unstable when they have an unsuitable balance of protons and neutrons; they emit excess energy as radiation and change into another element.

rubric.why: The nuclear balance of protons and neutrons explains nuclear instability.
rubric.how: Describe an unsuitable balance of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

rubric.why: Unstable nuclei release excess energy.
rubric.description: State what an unstable nucleus emits.
rubric.how: State that it emits excess energy as radiation.

rubric.why: The section explains that emission transforms the element during radioactive decay.
rubric.how: State that the nucleus changes into another element.

modelAnswer: Radioactive nuclei have an unsuitable balance of protons and neutrons and are unstable.
They emit excess energy in the form of radiation.
During radioactive decay, the radioactive element is transformed into another chemical element.

written.text: How does the theory of atomic structure explain the ionization of atoms by a radioactive isotope?
written.finalAnswer: Radiation from a radioactive source can collide with an atom and, if it has enough energy, force one or more electrons away. The atom then becomes a positively charged ion (cation).

rubric.why: The explanation must identify radiation from the source as the cause.
rubric.how: State that radiation emitted from a radioactive source acts on the atom.

rubric.why: An electron must receive enough energy to leave its atom.
rubric.how: Mention that the radiation must have enough energy to remove an electron.

rubric.why: Ionization here occurs when electron(s) are removed.
rubric.description: Describe what happens to the electron(s).
rubric.how: Explain that radiation can collide with the atom and force one or more electrons away.

rubric.why: Losing negative charge leaves the atom positively charged.
rubric.how: State that the atom becomes a positive ion or cation.

modelAnswer: Radiation emitted from a radioactive source can collide with an atom.
If it has enough energy, it forces one or more electrons away from the atom.
The atom then becomes a positively charged ion (cation).

written.text: What is radioactivity? Explain any three applications of radioactive isotopes.
written.finalAnswer: Radioactivity is the process of emission of radiation by an unstable isotope. Radioactive isotopes are used in medical imaging and to diagnose and treat diseases, including cancer and thyroid disorders; carbon-14 is used in radiocarbon dating to find the age of organic material; and radioactive isotopes are used to test the strength of metals and concrete mixtures.

rubric.how: Provide three distinct, relevant uses.

examTips: Expect short questions asking for the definition of isotopes, radioactivity or radioactive decay, or the neutron number of an isotope.
In constructed and descriptive answers, clearly connect unstable nuclei with emission of radiation, and radiation with transformation into another element.
For applications, name each use and briefly explain it; for example, carbon-14 dating estimates the age of organic material.
For a relative atomic mass calculation, show the mass × abundance products, their sum, division by 100 for percentage abundances, and the final rounded answer.
For ionization, show the full sequence: radiation supplies enough energy, an electron is removed, and a positive ion (cation) forms.

explain.title: What are isotopes?
explain.body: “Atoms of the same element having different number of neutrons in their nuclei are called isotopes.” Isotopes have the same atomic number but can have different mass numbers.

explain.title: Why are their properties alike and different?
explain.body: “Since the chemical properties of the elements are determined by the number of electrons, all three isotopes will show almost the same chemical behaviour, although their physical properties may be different.” Their different neutron numbers mean different masses.

explain.title: Radioactivity and radioactive decay
explain.body: “This process of emission of radiation is called radioactivity and the isotope which emits energy is called radioactive isotope.” When a radioactive element emits radiation and changes into another element, the process is called radioactive decay.

explain.title: Uses of radioactive isotopes
explain.body: They are used for medical imaging and diagnosing or treating disease. Carbon-14 is used to estimate the age of organic material. Radioactive isotopes can also be used to test the strength of metals and concrete mixtures.

explain.title: Ionization by radiation
explain.body: Radiation with enough energy can force one or more electrons away from an atom. Since the atom loses negative charge, it becomes a positively charged ion called a cation.

mistakes: Do not confuse atomic number with mass number: neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
Do not say isotopes have different numbers of protons; isotopes of one element have the same atomic number.
Do not claim isotopes have exactly the same physical properties; their masses and physical properties may differ.
Do not call every isotope radioactive; the section says some nuclei are unstable, while others are stable.
In ionization, show that an electron is removed and the atom becomes a positive ion, not a negative ion.
When finding relative atomic mass from percentages, divide the weighted sum by 100 and show the working.
